analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum nurse and aide staffing levels at Medicare- and Medicaid-funded nursing homes and requires public posting of staffing.
analysis.headline: Introduced with six Democratic cosponsors on September 13, 2000, the bill was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written the first minimum staffing ratios into federal law for every nursing home that takes Medicare or Medicaid money. Nursing homes would have to keep at least one licensed nurse on duty for every 15 residents during the day, 20 in the evening, and 30 overnight, and one hands-on caregiver for every 5 residents during the day, 10 in the evening, and 15 overnight. Facilities would also have to post their actual staffing levels, shift by shift, where residents and families can see them, and maintain key nursing administrators full time. Federal payments would be adjusted to help cover the added cost.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and their families, who would get guaranteed staffing levels and, for the first time, the ability to see on a posted notice how many caregivers are actually on duty on each shift before choosing or evaluating a home. Nurses and certified nurse aides would also benefit from higher demand for their work and from rules that stop administrators from being counted as caregivers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires every Medicare- and Medicaid-funded nursing facility to have at least one licensed nurse on duty for every 15 residents during the day, 20 in the evening, and 30 at night, and one direct caregiver (a certified nurse assistant or licensed nurse providing care) for every 5 residents by day, 10 in the evening, and 15 at night.
Stops facilities from padding their staffing numbers: administrative staff, food preparers, housekeeping, laundry, and maintenance workers cannot be counted toward the required caregiving ratios.

Requires facilities to conspicuously post, in a uniform format visible to residents, families, and prospective residents, the number of caregivers on the premises, the resident-to-nurse and resident-to-caregiver ratios, and the current resident count for each shift, and to keep that information available for at least a year.

Requires facilities to maintain a full-time director of nursing services (a registered nurse), plus an assistant director, a director of in-service education, and a clinical nursing supervisor on each shift, with limits on one person holding multiple roles.
Lets the Secretary of Health and Human Services set higher staffing minimums for facilities with sicker residents, and preserves states' ability to set stricter standards of their own.

Directs Medicare payment rates to be adjusted for the cost of meeting the staffing requirements, and requires Medicaid rates to take those costs into account, so facilities are paid for meeting the new standards.

Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to report to Congress within a year on whether enough trained caregiving personnel exist to meet the requirements, including steps to attract and retain them.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home operators, who would bear the cost of hiring more licensed nurses, aides, and nursing administrators. Federal and state governments would also pay more, since the bill requires Medicare payment adjustments and Medicaid rates that account for the cost of meeting the new staffing levels.

drawbacks.text: The bill would raise nursing homes' labor costs substantially, and the bill itself acknowledges the workforce may be inadequate by requiring a federal report on the adequacy of available personnel and steps to attract and retain caregivers; if enough trained nurses and aides cannot be hired, facilities could face fines or closures rather than better care.

Higher staffing costs flow partly into public budgets: the bill requires Medicare payment adjustments and Medicaid rates that take the new staffing costs into account, meaning federal and state taxpayers would pick up a share of the bill.

An industry complaint would be that uniform federal ratios ignore differences between facilities, and the bill gives smaller facilities (under 100 beds) flexibility on some administrative roles but no scaling relief on the core care ratios.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise is strong: independent of this bill, researchers and regulators have repeatedly linked low nursing home staffing to preventable injuries, pressure sores, and neglect, and the bill's posted-disclosure requirement would give families information they currently have no easy way to get. The genuine risks are on the supply side: ratios without a workforce plan can push marginal facilities toward closure and drive costs into Medicare and Medicaid rather than quality. The bill partially hedges by funding the requirements through payment adjustments and ordering a workforce report before the rules take effect two years after enactment, but it does not itself create the caregivers it mandates.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the House in mid-September 2000 and referred to the Ways and Means and Commerce committees, then to a Commerce subcommittee, and neither committee ever held a hearing or vote before the 106th Congress ended in early January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the Quality Care for Nursing Home Patients Act of 2000 on September 13, 2000, joined by six cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, the Commerce Committee, for consideration of the provisions under each committee's jurisdiction.
On October 19, 2000, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, its last recorded action.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators are better off: no hearing or vote ever happened, so no facility had to add nurses, aides, or administrators, and nothing had to be posted for residents and families to see. Residents and families gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All seven original supporters were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced far enough for a vote that would have shown how the parties split.

industries.note: Most nursing facilities, particularly for-profit chains, run on lean staffing, and this bill would have mandated specific nurse and aide ratios, banned counting administrators as caregivers, and required public posting of actual staffing by shift. Their interest in the bill as written ran against residents' access to more hands-on care, since compliance meant hiring staff they had avoided paying for.

The bill would have created demand for far more direct-care staff, prohibited counting non-caregiving work toward the ratios, and required a federal report on attracting and retaining caregiving personnel. Better staffing levels would also have eased workload for the caregivers already on the floor.

Taxpayers would have paid more through required Medicare payment adjustments and Medicaid rates that account for staffing costs, in exchange for care standards that could reduce preventable injuries and hospital transfers that also bill public programs.
